questions.stem: A 59-year-old man was seen with a recurrence of fevers and chills. He was on day 7 of a 2-week course of doxycycline (100 mg BID) for presumed Lyme disease. He was a deer hunter from Nantucket, who had first presented with a 5-day history of a circular rash on his back, associated with fevers and chills. The rash had cleared, and his systemic symptoms had settled on starting doxycycline.
questions.lead_in: What is the most appropriate treatment?

options.text: Atovaquone and azithromycin PO for 7 days
Ceftriaxone IV followed by doxycycline PO to complete 21 days
Clindamycin and chloroquine PO for 7 days

questions.explanation: Atovaquone and azithromycin PO for 7 days The most likely explanation is a co-infection with babesiosis. Ixodes scapularis is the vector for Lyme disease, human anaplasmosis, and babesiosis. It is likely that he was appropriately diagnosed with early Lyme disease (given classic bull’s-eye skin rash). Although he initially responded, he had a deterioration which is classic for co-infection with babesiosis. Babesia has a slightly longer incubation period and tends to occur later. In contrast to anaplasmosis, Babesia is not covered by doxycycline. Chloroquine has no activity against Babesia either. The current recommended therapy is atovaquone and azithromycin for 7–10 days.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 1 Q32

questions.stem: A 54-year-old farmer in Massachusetts became acutely unwell in late August. He had had nonspecific symptoms which came on gradually for 1 week, including fatigue, anorexia, and headache. He then developed high sustained fevers, sweats, myalgia, and dark urine. His medical history included splenectomy following a road traffic accident 15 years earlier, hypercholesterolemia, and hypertension. He was up to date with his immunizations and took amlodipine and atorvastatin. He had not traveled outside of the US in the preceding 10 years and had not left Massachusetts in the preceding 6 months. He lived with his wife and two teenage daughters, all of whom were well. On examination, he was visibly icteric, with pale conjunctivae, and was dyspneic at rest. His temperature was 38.5°C, heart rate 124 beats per minute, blood pressure 85/50 mmHg, respiratory rate 34 breaths per minute. He had inspiratory crackles to midzones bilaterally. His liver was palpable 2 cm below the right costal margin and his spleen tip was also palpable. Investigations: HIV Ag/Ab negative, hepatitis C IgG negative, HBS negative Hemoglobin 63 g/L (130–180) White blood cell count 17.6 ×109/L Neutrophil count 14.3 ×109/L Platelet count 112 ×109/L Serum creatinine 213 μmol/L (60–110) Serum alkaline phosphatase 167 U/L (45–105) Blood film:
questions.lead_in: What is the most appropriate treatment?
questions.explanation: Quinine sulfate plus clindamycin In asplenic patients infection with Babesia microti can be severe, with intense hemolysis leading to severe anemia, jaundice, and renal failure. DIC, ARDS, and noncardiac pulmonary edema are described. Diagnosis is by microscopic examination of a Giemsa-stained thin blood film. The blood film shows a typical tetrad of merozoites within an erythrocyte (“Maltese cross”) as well as multiple ring forms. First-line treatment for severe babesiosis or infection in immunosuppressed patients is with quinine and clindamycin. Treatment is recommended for at least 6 weeks. Blood transfusion and intensive care support may be required. (Image from Assessments. In Cohen J, Powderly W , Opal S, eds. Infectious Diseases. 4th ed. Elsevier; 2017.)
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 6 Q50

questions.stem: A 19-year-old man presented with a 2-day history of fever, weakness, and dark-colored urine. Ten days earlier he had been given a clinical diagnosis of erythema migrans for a new target-shaped lesion on his thigh. He was on day 10 of a 14-day course of doxycycline. He had no known drug allergies. He initially felt better and the lesions disappeared but then deteriorated symptomatically. On physical examination, his temperature was 38.5°C. He was visibly jaundiced, and he had tender hepatosplenomegaly. No rashes were seen, and the remainder of the exam was normal. Investigations: Hemoglobin 8.7 g/dL Bilirubin 3.5 mg/dL (60 μmol/L) Peripheral smear:
questions.lead_in: What is the best empiric therapy?
questions.explanation: Atovaquone plus azithromycin The patient has babesiosis and was co-infected with Lyme disease. The image shows Maltese crosses in a patient with active symptoms and risk factors for babesiosis. Asymptomatic disease does not require treatment. For mild disease, atovaquone plus azithromycin for 7–10 days is the treatment of choice. Remember the co-infections that can occur: babesiosis and Lyme disease. A phrase to help you remember: “Anna gives lime juice to her babies” (anaplasmosis, Lyme, babesiosis). Quiz 8 Answers
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 8 Q16

questions.question: Patient on expedition in Washington state. Fever, splenomegaly, thrombocytopenia, cytolysis.

parts.text: What is the clinical entity?
What is the organism involved?
How to do a quick Dx?
Following the treatment, the patient develops a reaction with fever and pain, what is this syndrome?

cohort_answer.text:
Clinical entity: Tick borne relapsing fever. Could be babesiosis, but not common in Washington state. Also part 3 of the question points to borrelia infection. cyclic fever, flu like symptoms, chill phase, western US/BC in rustic cabins
Organism: Borellia hermsii
Quick Dx: Blood smear to look for spirochetes (better if done with first episode, less likely to see on recurrent episodes)
Syndrome after treatment: Jarisch-Herxheimer reaction. Tx: doxy, macrolides, penicillin

questions.question: [image-based question: Picture of maltese cross in patient travelling through the Eastern seaboard.]

parts.text: Name the organisms (species level).
Name the vector to the species level.
What are risk factors for severe babesia (four).
What is the treatment for severe babesia.
What other organisms can be transmitted by the same vector.

cohort_answer.text: Organism: Babesia microti (can look like P. falciparum on smear). Vector: Ixodes scapularis. Risk factors for severe babesia: Asplenia, >50 yo, malignancy, immunocompromised state, HIV/AIDS, liver disease, TNF inhibitors. Treatment for severe babesia: Quinine + clindamycin (atovaquone + azithro for mild-mod). Other organisms same vector: Borrelia burgdorferi, Anaplasma phagocytophilum, Borrelia mayonii, Ehrlichia

questions.question: 32M who went to Southwest Ontario hiking. Suffered an MI and required multiple transfusions. You are shown a picture of his blood smear.

parts.text: What is the name and genus of the species AND another pathogen of the same genus but different species
What is the treatment?
What adjunctive therapy can you consider in cases of uncontrolled hemolysis and disease?

questions.model_answer:
a) Genus/species: Babesia microti (most common cause of babesiosis in North America, including southwestern Ontario tick-endemic areas). Another pathogen, same genus different species: Babesia duncani (or Babesia divergens, more common in Europe).
b) Treatment: atovaquone plus azithromycin (standard regimen for mild-to-moderate disease); for severe disease, clindamycin plus quinine.
c) Adjunctive therapy for uncontrolled hemolysis/high parasitemia: red blood cell exchange transfusion.

questions.question: Lady went hiking and camping in Maine (USA) and presents with flu-like illness. Blood smear shows maltese cross

parts.text: Name the pathogen
What is the treatment of the patient?
What are two methods of acquisition?
Name two other pathogens transmitted by the same vector.

cohort_answer.text: Babesia microti. Treatment: Mild - Atovaquone 750mg q12h + Azithromycin 500mg day1, 250mg day2 on, x7-10d; Severe - Quinine + Clindamycin (+/- exchange transfusion). Acquisition: Tick bite (Ixodes scapularis), Transfusion. Other pathogens same vector: Borrelia burgdorferi, Anaplasma (also Powassan virus)

questions.question: 82 yo F travel in NE US (Hartford?). Develops fever, chills. [image-based question: blood film shown with intra-erythrocytic trophozoites, Maltese cross]

parts.text: What is the Diagnosis (Genus, Species)?
How is it transmitted (Vector genus, species)?
What are four risk factors for developing severe illness?
What is first line therapy for severe illness?
What other organisms are transmitted by this vector (Name two)?

cohort_answer.text: Babesia microti. Vector: Ixodes scapularis (deer tick/black-legged tick) - transmits Borrelia burgdorferi/miyamotoi, Powassan encephalitis virus, Anaplasma phagocytophilum, Babesia microti, Ehrlichia. Risk factors for severe illness: Asplenia; HIV; Malignancy; Transplant; TNF-alpha inhibitors; B cell depletion; Advanced age. Severe babesiosis often in older/immunocompromised patients, associated with parasitemia >=4% (can occur <4%); exchange transfusion considered for parasitemia >10% and/or severe hemolytic anemia or severe pulmonary/renal/hepatic compromise. First line severe therapy: Clindamycin 600mg PO/IV TID-QID + Quinine 650mg PO TID-QID x7-10 days +/- exchange transfusion. Mild-moderate: Atovaquone 750mg PO BID x7 days + azithromycin 500-1000mg once then 250mg daily x6 days. (Mnemonic for tickborne co-infections: "Ana gives lime juice to her babies" - anaplasmosis, Lyme, babesiosis.) Other organisms from this vector: Borrelia burgdorferi, Borrelia miyamotoi, B. mayonii, Babesia, Powassan/deer tick virus (POWV lineage II), Anaplasma, Ehrlichia muris eauclairensis (E. chaffeensis and E. ewingii are from Lone Star tick).

questions.question: Guy who had CABG in Massachusetts, then decides that it is a good idea to go hiking. Now has fever, myalgia and severe hemolytic anemia. Gives picture of blood film showing maltese cross. [image-based question: blood film showing Maltese cross]

parts.text: Name the most common species AND another within the same genus that occurs in US
Name the vector
What is the treatment regimen
What is another treatment option if severe hemolytic anemia

cohort_answer.text: Species: Babesia microti, Babesia duncani. Vector: Ixodes scapularis. Severe treatment: Atovaquone 750mg PO BID and azithromycin 500mg IV day 1 then 250mg IV daily (continue 500mg if immunocompromised); duration 7-10 days, unless high risk features (B cell cancer/rituximab, malignancy with asplenia, HIV, SOT/BMT) then minimum 6 weeks, and 2 weeks with cleared parasitemia; milder infection can treat with all oral regimen; alternative regimen clindamycin and quinine. Other treatment for severe hemolysis: Exchange transfusion if severe hemolysis with Hgb <100, parasitemia >10%, organ impairment

questions.question: Q68 (2016 AM, 2003 PM, 2008). 82F travel in NE US (Hartford?) develops fever, chills. Blood film with intra-erythrocytic trophozoites (Maltese cross)

parts.text: A) What is the diagnosis (genus and species)?
B) How is it transmitted (vector genus, species)?
C) What are 4 risk factors for developing severe illness?
D) What is first line for severe illness?
E) What other organisms are transmitted by this vector (name 2)?

cohort_answer.text: A) Babesia microti. B) Ixodes scapularis. C) Asplenia; HIV; Malignancy; Transplant; TNFalpha inhibitors; Advanced age. D) 2020 IDSA Guidelines preferred for all severity levels: Atovaquone 750mg PO Q12h plus azithromycin 500mg PO day1 then 250mg Q24h x7-10 days; Clindamycin plus quinine alternative. E) Borrelia burgdorferi; Anaplasma; Powassan fever.

questions.question: Trivia: Seven tropical infections that can be diagnosed with peripheral blood smear (Giemsa)

parts.text: Name the seven infections

cohort_answer.text: African/American trypanosomiasis, Babesia, Bartonella (bacilliformis - Oroya fever), Filariasis, Malaria, TBRF (tick-borne relapsing fever), LBRF (louse-borne relapsing fever) (also Histoplasmosis, Leptospirosis mentioned)
